en: 1. Nidānakāṇḍa 1.1. Introduction [Success! Homage to the Omniscient One.
Bestowing supreme glory, he surpassed the Creator; casting away darkness, he eclipsed the sun;
dispelling the summer heat, he conquered the beautiful moon.
He who has no equal here is honored as an Arhat;
by him alone, for the benefit of human beings,
the discourse on the evolution and dissolution of the world was set forth, and that is now being described.
For even when there is something to be revealed, one who resorts to silence does not enter the supreme path of the virtuous;
this [speech] is like the flame of a lamp for embodied beings.
Placed at the forefront, it dispels the darkness of ignorance;
for this very reason, it is not fitting for the wise to turn their backs on its illumination. [1.1.3]
Just as a lotus bed, resting upon beautiful stalks, partakes in great splendor, so too does this narrative,
from its very beginning, possess the character of an introduction like a well-fashioned ear-ornament.
Let that which is captivating be placed within the range of hearing.
Thus ends the first rest-period, named the Introduction.
1.2. There was a place called Kumārodaya, its sides surrounded by a row of clouds that possessed the beauty of vast and lofty *śāla* trees.
The city of the great seer Kapila, situated deep within the sky, was inhabited by those of exalted intellect and fervor;
it captivated the mind with its very mass, which was white and lofty.
It rendered fruitful the clouds that had approached Mount Kailāsa out of delusion, either to assume its cloud-like splendor or to fulfill their own expectations. [1.2.2]
There, shining with the radiance of jewels, darkness found no place, just as poverty finds none,
due to the satisfaction derived from living among the most excellent citizens.
The splendor shone forth as if with a smile,
as it bore the beauty of jewels upon every house, on the altars, arches, and lion-heads. [1.2.3]
Seeing nothing else in the world as their equal, they vied with one another for their own palaces;
they surpassed the lotuses by means of the moon-like faces of their beloveds. [1.2.4]
Where even the sun,
having arrived, departed toward the western ocean to embrace the waters, as if out of a desire for heat after being treated with contempt.
"This moon has been reduced by the people to the status of a mere illustration for the fame earned by the Śākyas"—
thus [they cried] with banners bearing beautiful, fluttering pennants.
Even though the moon,
residing in its silver palace, made the night-blooming lilies laugh with its rays during the night, it raised them up as if to wipe away the mark upon its own face.
Having been consecrated upon the heads of the kings, he assumed the luster of a lotus during the day within his golden palaces, where the rays of the sun had already reached him.
The king named Śuddhodana, a kinsman of the Sun, adorned that city as the sovereign of kings, like a pond with its depths clear and its white lotuses in full bloom. [1.2.8]
Though he is the most excellent of mountain-lords, he is indeed possessed of wings;
though he has set forth his gifts, he is not overcome by pride;
and though he is a sovereign, he always casts an equal gaze upon all.
Though gentle by nature, he possessed vast majesty;
for when the lordly elephants of his enemies were struck by his arm and fell upon the battlefields, [they could not withstand him].

Having cast off their enemies through excessive valor, they prostrated with their heads—adorned with clusters of pearls that had been disgorged—as if with handfuls of flowers offered out of devotion. [1.2.1
Like the sun after a great eclipse,
he illuminated the people on all sides,
pointing out the paths worthy of being followed.
By his policy, dharma, artha, and kāma did not encroach upon one another's domain; yet they strove together,
as it were, for the sake of fierce success.
They became even more radiant within their own respective domains.
[1.2.12] That one of exalted nature, having been made the foremost by his ministers— who were both noble in number and beyond counting— [proceeded].

Like the moon amidst those who were not made so, the King, the Lord of the Śākyas, shone forth all the more; his splendor spread with an exceeding brilliance. [1.2.13] His splendor was diffused with an exceeding splendor.
Like the radiance of the sun dispelling the power of darkness,
she became the foremost goddess among the entire host of goddesses; though appearing as illusion, she was indeed free from illusion.
Active in seeking the welfare of her subjects like a mother,
following her elders with devotion like a faithful servant,
she shed her luster upon the family of her lord like the goddess Lakṣmī.
In this world, she became the embodiment of the supreme deity;
though the conduct of women is always as darkness, yet having attained her, it shone forth intensely.
For having approached the bright crescent of the moon at night, one does not likewise fall into total darkness; thus, this [self] is difficult to deceive regarding that which transcends the senses.
[1.2.16] This [self] is difficult to deceive regarding that which transcends the senses.
As if thinking, "I am unable to unite with the common folk," she abandoned her subtle nature and assumed a beautiful form directly ordained by Dharma. [1.2.17]
Then, having passed away from Tuṣita, the supreme Bodhisattva, illuminating the three worlds,
entered her womb while remaining mindful.
Like the king of serpents in the Nandā cave,
the guardians of the world approached the sole lord of the world, heaven, for the purpose of providing protection. [1.2.18]
For although the rays of the moon shine everywhere,
they attain a special distinction upon Mount Kailāsa;
even Māyā, bearing him within her womb, [attains a special distinction].
Like a row of clouds with the play of lightning,
she became one who pacified the heat of poverty for people everywhere through the rains of her gifts. [1.2.20]
And he too, emerging from his mother’s womb like the sun from a cloud at dawn,
dispelled the darkness with his shimmering rays.
He made the world radiant with gold;
being borne by the foremost of the gods,
he delighted them with the masses of light-rays emanating from his body.
At the festival of his birth, the earth, like a crest-jewel upon the mountain peaks, surpassed the newly risen moon in splendor as it rested above the mass of twilight clouds.
Adorned with scattered flowers, she trembled;
the ocean, its beauty enhanced by the application of its own foam, danced with its hands of waves. [1.2.23]
A breeze blew, carrying the lovely fragrance drawn forth by flowering trees, to be enjoyed by the limbs of people,
accompanied by the music of drums and the dances of the celestial beauties.
The sky shone with celestial chariots made of flowers;
through the power of the seasons' perfect transformation, the three worlds rejoiced, their afflictions dispelled.
The Śākya clan rejoiced all the more, its splendor enhanced by that jewel of a birth,
as the elders beheld those goals of his already accomplished.
They gave him the name Siddhārtha;
endowed with such qualities, he shone exceedingly, like a golden ornament set with excellent jewels. [1.2.26]

Having thus received the true prophecy from the Lord of Sages, he will become the sole protector of the world; like a wish-fulfilling gem whose value has been recognized, he will [bring benefit] to all people.
He became a worthy vessel for the world's esteem.
Then, growing like a tree of paradise together with the desires of the people, he flourished.
Having made his own splendor common to all,
he caused the world to appear as if it were a gift from the Giver of Wealth;
[he made it] beautiful with the arts of knowledge in its entirety—
The beauty of fresh youth, as if filled with passion, embraced him with intense joy as he bore a body endowed with all auspicious marks.
Then, as a youth, he— by means of his virtues and the rays of his fame, which made the entire abode of the world white—
[surpassed] the glories of the foremost among mortals and gods.
"The sun has outshone the stars"—
having formed this suspicion that "this man, whose sole devotion is to Dharma, might go to the forest," the King of the Śākyas then [acted].
He united him with brides who brought victory to the King of Love;
the moon, repeatedly filling itself with its own splendor, [shone].
As if out of a desire to conquer the faces of his daughters-in-law,
he— having never known equality with them and now rendered utterly pale with shame— underwent emaciation once again, and that all at once. [1.2.32]
Surely the Creator, through the practice of yoga, having perfected his rules of artistry, fashioned those women of graceful bodily splendor from among others.
[1.2.33] Possessing a form desirable even to celestial nymphs,
he was charming with the graceful gestures inspired by them;
though full of amorous playfulness, he was nonetheless endowed with the deportment of a king.
Upon seeing mortals struck by old age, disease, and death, he found no pleasure in the duties of the householder’s life. The second rest, titled "The Birth of the Prince."

1.3. Seeking the attainment of Buddhahood and searching for escape from suffering, though exhorted by the lords of the gods, he abandoned his kingdom and adorned the forest like a scent-elephant. [1.3.1]

There, covered by garments of copper-red hue offered by the gods, he whose hair was shorn assumed the supreme splendor of the sun garlanded by the clouds of twilight. Having attended upon other teachers, he found no delight in their doctrines.
For the sun is not instructed by a firefly on how to rise.
[1.3.3] Having approached the royal capital of Great Enlightenment, which is worthy of the greatest veneration, he achieved the defeat of the enemy Māra with the sword of patience. [1.3.4]
There, in order to extract the great nectar inaccessible even to gods and daityas,
the sovereign mountain of knowledge then churned the ocean of the knowable;
abandoning the two extremes of truth as things to be discarded, and taking up that which is to be grasped, it brought it forth.
Having conquered his enemies—the faults without exception—he attained the supreme state.
Then, as if it were the news of his victory, the radiance of his body surged forth;
illuminating the entire world, it filled it with overflowing joy.
As if her body had been anointed with unguents by her, the Earth, in order to celebrate a great festival,
caused the mountains to dance by imitating her own graceful movements.
Taking jewels as offerings with her hands consisting of shimmering waves, she—
The ocean, with its foam as a smile, rose up as if to honor him.
There, the sky, serving as the arena for the spectacle, became filled with the sound of lovely songs and the charming dancing of the gods.
Then, for a certain time, he overlooked his progeny who were devoted to their homes;
for the glorious cloud, the benefactor of mankind, rains nectar when the proper time has arrived.
At the request of Brahmā, he set the wheel of Dharma in motion upon the earth.
When great beings seek the supreme goal, by good fortune there arises the practice of noble deeds.
Having received the light of the speech of the Sun-like Victor, the five monks, together with the gods, had the mass of darkness dispelled and directly realized the auspicious Dharma. [1.3.12–13]
This news was proclaimed by the terrestrial yakṣas as if out of curiosity;
it ascended to the Akaniṣṭha heaven by means of a series of divine stairways.
While this festival of Dharma was underway, accompanied by the sounds of celestial drums, [the news spread].
The earth, clothed in the waters of the various oceans and possessing the moving clouds as her breasts,
displayed that marvel to all embodied beings, as if to show it to them;
and the radiance of the Sugata dispelled the darkness even in other worlds.
Then he awakened the true Dharma for the Kāśyapas along with their disciples;
surrounded by them, he shone even more brightly, like the moon together with the stars.
Thereafter, he demonstrated the truths to King Bimbisāra.
For other people follow the path that the best person has already traveled.
Moreover, by bringing Śāradvatīputra and Kolita into discipleship, the Jina shone even more brilliantly.
Mount Meru does not shine forth at all until the sun and the moon move in their clockwise orbits. [1.3.19] 1.4. The Defeat of the Heretics.
Thus, when his teaching had come to be honored by the heads of those possessed of great virtues,
the sun reached its rising.
The doctrine of the heretics vanished like darkness;
in some places among the low-born, those who had conceived great greed were like day-gnats finding their opportunity.
The entire assemblies of rival sectarians cried out in protest against those various words of the Tathāgata which contradicted their own tenets:
"This could not be Mount Meru, nor this earth, nor even this ocean! [1.4.2]
"The sun and the moon, beautiful in their fixed courses, are not the eyes of the world;
for if Īśāna were the creator of the world, he would not be like a potter.
Yet, some indeed say that because of the existence of sentient beings (*sattva*), this world speaks of Īśvara as its creator. [1.4.3]
Rain consists of water, clouds of earth, lightning of fire, and sound of air; with what is each associated here, and what is conjoined with what?
That the clouds rain, auspicious with their deep resonance and the play of lightning—[what is the nature of this union]?
Therefore, apart from a cause, others maintain that there is such a restriction of intrinsic nature:
at the arising of a kalpa, this world, which did not previously exist, does not come into being;
and at the end of a kalpa, no dissolution occurs for anything whose continuity has ceased.
Others, however, say that it is not so; for like the appearance and disappearance of objects day and night, it is joined with the arising and destruction of both the existent and the non-existent.
This is neither this world, nor the next, nor a mother.

"Beings are neither fathers nor non-fathers, yet they are known by the world; this is indeed an error, and since that object does not exist, others say the world is like a painting in the sky. [1.4.6]
If everything arises from a Lord, then surely He too must arise in the same way; thus there would be no stability.
If [you argue] that this is not so because of His eternity, then by the same logic, the world would also be eternal, due to its conformity with the nature of its cause.
Furthermore, the claim that an eternal being possesses the act of producing is false; otherwise, even desire could be something produced.
Due to its constant proximity at the time of birth, everything might either always exist or perhaps never at all.

The clouds, consisting of the agitation of the elements, are water-shedders; because they consist predominantly of water and arise from those causes, they are joined with the thunder and lightning along with the thick masses of cloud.
If this collection of clouds and so forth were to exist in such a manner, what would be inconsistent here?
If not, then there would be no cause at all for anything to arise anywhere. From whence would these manifestations and disappearances come, when everything is eternal?
For nothing unprecedented could be equal to the sun in its power to manifest and conceal;

yet beings and other things undergo transformation. Now, if it is argued that everything has indeed reached a state of impermanence and thus no eternal things exist at all, this pair of claims is contradictory. [1.4.9]

If everything does not exist, then even the means of valid cognition (*pramā*) would not exist; from what, then, would the fact that "it does not exist" be established, by which it could be determined that "it exists"? Or else, how could that [means of cognition] itself be impossible without it? Since nothing is perceived anywhere, how can this [charge of] undermining all perception be sustained?
"For all cognitions are indeed erroneous; what kind of cognition could now remain as a locus for error?
Having thus perceived the path of the false heretics as resembling a precipice, the best of sages set out to lead the world upon the level path.

Through this discourse, he correctly explained the world— along with its causes and lack of causes, as well as its birth and destruction— as it truly exists. The Fourth Interlude, titled "The Defeat of the Heretics."
And first is the Section on the Introduction (Nidānakāṇḍa).
2. The Section on the State of Evolution (Vivartamānāvasthākāṇḍa) 2.1. The Arising of Deities Residing in Space:
While the world was evolving, [there appeared] a radiant...
At first, a celestial chariot, its canopy shining above the dwellings of the people, rose up like the orb of the sun produced by the karma of its own constituent elements, belonging to the Creator.
Then, even though he has passed away from that abode of the Ābhāsvara deities, a certain being, assuming a body made radiant by the arising of his karma, enters [the womb] and is adorned.
He became like the lord of stars amidst white clouds;
attaining perfection through the bliss of meditative absorption, he remained fully concentrated there for ten eons.
Let there indeed be incomparable manifestations;
how could there be any transformation in the greatness of the Existent? At the end of that, the one who was dissatisfied reflected:
"O, may other embodied beings also become thus!
Surrounded by the gods born from his own karma and arisen from his own body, he shone like the moon encircled by the host of stars. [2.1.4]
Beholding them arisen together with his own mind,
he attained the conceit, "I am the creator"; fie upon that ignorance, wherein even great-souled ones fall!
Neither by the principle of "the crow and the palm fruit" nor out of delusion did even the gods,
having observed him as previously described and possessed of great supernatural power, acknowledge him as the agent.
What is surprising in this, that people follow what is highly esteemed by the foremost out of excessive admiration? Now, as for other abodes of Brahmā born of good karma—
The sky bore an ever-increasing array of celestial bodies,
as if its curiosity had been aroused by the sight of his birth;
and more than ten kalpas passed from that time.
Having taken as their model Brahmā and the other gods together with their celestial abodes through their past deeds, the deities of the Brahmakāyika realm were constructed along with their palaces;
these appeared like reflections arisen in the mirror of the sky. [2.1.8]
The celestial chariots of the domestic priests clung to their shadows.
Adorned above with parasols like the temples of the God of Love,
the abodes of the Vaśavartin gods shone forth, arisen from the karma of those who have attained mastery over their desires.
Or perhaps they came into being through their own past actions, competing with these [palaces],
serving as dwellings for the pleasure of creation and resplendent with throngs of Apsarases;
they rose up as if submerged in the ocean of the sky by means of their karma.
Resembling masses of foam, they shone with the beautiful abodes of the Tuṣita gods.
Then, having arisen from their own seeds as swarms of bees that were gods and goddesses,
they adorned the lake of the sky— the dwellings of the Yāma gods— like lotuses.
There are six bodies here, which arise in each successive eon, one after another, descending lower and lower;
they are fashioned as if by a ritual for their descent into the lower realms.
They shone, resting upon the steps of the divided stairway.
[2.1.14] In the second book, the first rest, titled "The Arising of the Gods Abiding in the Sky."
2.2. Pṛthivīnivāsaḥ:
Then, remembering their former births and desiring to behold Mount Meru and other such peaks, the sons of Yama emerged from their dwellings like rays of light. [2.2.1]
"Sumeru was Śakrapūra here; Yugandhara was Sāgara here"—
thus do they recollect their former lives here in detail.
From his body the wind emerged;
that air blew above, below, and all around,
and it attained a supreme increase.
They become supremely capable without difficulty;
it is no cause for wonder that those whose souls are exalted by greatness [act thus]. Then, with dense clouds thundering steadily above him...
The water was released in abundance from all sides by those whose ornaments were as beautiful as the flickering play of lightning;
for there is no deficiency in the act of giving among the most exalted.
Even though it was bottomless and profound,
the wind held back that water by surrounding it;
for those who have mastered their own minds are able to sustain even their enemies.
Nothing is more unbearable for the great-souled than this:
now this water has spread out on all sides,
dark as a peacock’s neck by its own power.
The sky shone as if it had been abandoned below by the clouds, who, desiring to reach his dwelling, remained at his feet;
for in due course, all beings had attained their essence within him.
Above the waters, a layer of mud formed,
identical in appearance to the milk that had turned solid within,
having spread out and cooled with its inner beauty revealed.
Then, once there, the artisan Wind, impelled by the sovereign power of karma, [prepared] with this clay for the vessel,
in order to fashion the world of the gods.
As if with hundreds of hands,
he proceeded to manifest Sumeru together with the oceans,
which was situated within a square enclosure; thus the wind blew.
Even the elephant of Indra yawned, as if to make the vault of the sky and the ocean one through his singular prowess,
divided by his own sevenfold movement.
Wandering even further in that same manner,
he created seven mountain ranges as well, beginning with Yugandhara, whose bodies were half-concealed by cool shadows.
Circling around the regions at the edge of the earth, which was situated below and perfectly circular, he seemed to be tracing out a line himself, as if to measure its extent.

[2.2.11] Having established the meeting of those two— the outer ocean of cool waters and this [inner ocean]— at the intermediate directions (vidik) between them, he created the outer reservoir of water together with the Cakravāla mountains.
As he created the four continents together with their thrones, he seemed, out of affection, to bestow the four directions upon them;
in due course, they came to consist of great jewels.
The nine lords of mountains, whose nature is earth, have been raised high by great beings; there is no path for women that does not lead to a low state. [2.3.13]
Seeing this world made high and low by the wind,
the clouds, as if concealing their own intent, appear to offer protection so that no slanderer may find an opportunity here.
They covered the entire expanse from the oceans to the sky with their waters.
[2.3.14] In the second book, the second rest-period titled "The Dwelling on Earth" concludes. 2.
2.3 The Rise of the God Residing in the Abode of the Naga Kings:
Now, as if to consecrate him in the sovereignty over all the mountains with the waters of the lord of the oceans, [the gods...]
It is completely encircled on all sides by the lords of the great mountain ranges, which stand firm outside its half-circle extending for a hundred thousand yojanas; there,
fatigue is ever-arisen due to the lack of any support.
As if thinking, "Let this not fall prostrate upon the earth," he seemed to support the vast expanse of the sky with his lofty peaks rising on all four sides.
For one who has attained a preeminent elevation beyond this world,
conduct that is improper and unequal to others is as if intended to conquer the universe in every direction.
It was beautiful, well-proportioned, and perfectly square;
it stood at the center for the sake of providing a dwelling for the gods, who had not yet attained the summit and whose upward-directed activities were still unfolding.
He possessed four folds of skin that had become like rings, bearing them just like a stūpa;
he was not bent anywhere due to being situated in the middle.
As if saying, "This very world has been surpassed by him," he delighted the quarters of the sky on all sides with his wondrous and exceedingly radiant form. [2.3.5]
Having become that very form— strewn with flowers, its body variegated by jewels rising and falling as they were set and removed—
the gods, including Indra, through their own past actions, [attained it].
They made Mount Sumeru their pleasure garden.
(This concludes the group of six verses. [2.3.6] || 6 ||

With its walls of śāla wood inlaid with many jewels, which served as festive mirrors for the wives of the mountain peaks, that city— with its gate-towers— seemed to scrape the very heavens as it rose upward.
[2.3.7] As if rising far above the tops of the assembly halls,
what further illustration could there be for this [mountain], other than through its own action, as if to say: "Having abandoned its own form"?
It was displayed by its own houses, constructed from the four great jewels, with pigeon-cots, *hari-ear* windows, and archways. [2.3.8]
Resplendent and crowded with many acts of devotion,
it was being performed as if by far-reaching banners,
having had the binding of the turban of office performed for the lordship of the city.
Her limbs were stained with the abundant pollen arising from flowers in the rivers, ponds, and groves;
and she was adorned with riches that appeared at her will.
With its internal splendor exalted by the objects of one's desires,
it is ever intent on dispelling the darkness by means of the radiance of various kinds of supreme jewels.
Capable of inducing sleep and awakening by means of night and day indicated by the closing and opening of the lotuses,
it is another [world] possessing the splendor of an incomparable manifestation of form.
Finding no suitable support on the earth,
they made Mount Sumeru their capital city, Sudarśana, which had become like a crown upon it. [2.3.12]

Even the Yugandhara and other mountains were led by the gods to become pleasure-mountains,
their slopes adorned by the Four Great Kings.
And previously, four [cities] attained the status of being preeminent cities by Purandara, as well as by other leaders,
even by such eminent ones as Kakutstha and Rājika.
Having attained sovereignty and adorned with virtuous policies,
both classes of gods conversed in many ways regarding their beloved departure. [2.3.14] Being bound by their affection for the journey—
Having gradually conciliated them with words, some entered the Sudharmā assembly hall— the ornament of the lord of the immortals— which was permitted by the members of the assembly. [2.3.15]
After a long time, other women from the inner apartments, having departed from here, pacified him after he had become enraged;
for it was not only our bodies that remained here.
But why are you so angry, O mind, when there is nothing else?
Others, with sweet voices, repeatedly striking the lute as it approaches their ears, sing melodious songs.
The foremost beauties of the city, possessing the splendor of full-bodied forms, sported like the goddesses of the bodiless god of love;
they traversed jewel-encrusted riverbanks in great chariots.
Having plunged into the rivers in jewel-boats swift as thought, some sported together with throngs of Apsarases,
incited by their mutual desire for victory.
Adorned with crest-ornaments that fill the ears,
most beautiful and yellowish-brown with nectar, they resounded with the songs of bees and cuckoos.
Others than the vice-regent went to the forest on a chariot procession;
some, having shaken off their enemies who had long been preparing for war, did so by means of various heroic exploits.
They experienced a festival during their entry into the city, which was celebrated by throngs of joyful apsarases;
these gods, so called because they play, remained unshaken even by their own enemies.
They did not grieve even as the eighteenth kalpa was coming to its end.
In the Second Book, the third rest, titled "The Rise of the Gods Dwelling on the Lord of Mountains."
2.4. In the two kalpas following that, there is the arising of mortals; having attained their physical forms, they are devoid of the distinctions of female, male, and neuter.
In that world, mortals moved about upon the surface of the sky like clouds,
by the radiance of their own bodies, as do the hosts of planets. Then, for them, this earth appeared as a shimmering entity.

Perceiving her to be most beautiful with a fragrant scent, a man, overcome by greed, carried her off; likewise did others do so, for people indeed adopt the conduct of those with whom they dwell. [2.4.2]
All mortals, having resorted to the practice of eating, experienced the loss of their radiance and the heaviness of their bodies; thus,
by relying on greed as the primary cause, calamity ensued.
Just as the six positions [of the planets] first occurred in the world,
so too did the Sun and Moon suddenly appear together between the two poles of the celestial sphere, joined by their respective latitudes and declinations.
With their side-long glances and beautiful eyes, these two shone intensely as they gazed far up into the sky. By this much, this person has been transformed; indeed, twenty kalpas have passed.
For at the rising of the methods that destroy darkness, those things existing as conventional reality quickly vanish.
The fourth rest, titled "The Arising of Mortals."
And the second is the section on the state of evolution.
